Herd Demography & Population Dynamics

Herd_Demography.Rmd

1. Choosing Your Mode: Manual Census vs. Automatic Cycle

When running calculate_population(), your first decision is whether to provide your own inventory numbers or let herdr model the farm’s herd structure automatically:

# Option A: Manual Census (Default)
calculate_population(automatic_cycle = FALSE)

# Option B: Automatic Biological Cycle
calculate_population(automatic_cycle = TRUE)

When to use automatic_cycle = FALSE (Manual Census)

  • Real-world farm records: Choose this when you have actual farm records, historical census data, or you already know the Annual Average Population (AAP) / standing barn places of every cohort.
  • Direct control: You fill in livestock_census.csv with each group present on the farm (e.g., 100 dairy cows, 27 replacement heifers, 35 feedlot calves). herdr uses your figures directly as declared.

When to use automatic_cycle = TRUE (Automatic Demographic Cycle)

  • Future scenario modeling & prospective studies: Choose this when planning farm expansions, simulating genetic or management improvements, or conducting prospective environmental impact assessments.
  • Breeding-only inventory: You only need to declare your adult breeding animals in livestock_census.csv (e.g., mature cows, breeding sows, ewes, or hens).
  • Automated biological pyramid: herdr automatically models the complete demographic flow: annual births, young animals retained to replace culled adults, and the average standing population in the fattening barn.

2. The Core Demographic Concept

Regardless of the species, livestock farm demography in herdr divides animals into two conceptual populations:

  1. The Breeding Base (Permanent Adults): Animals that live year-round on the farm generating offspring. Because they age, lose productivity, or are culled, a proportion must be replaced periodically to keep the herd size stable.
  2. The Offspring & Meat Flow (Temporal Cohorts): All young animals born on the farm. A fraction is retained as replacements to sustain the breeding base, while all remaining surplus animals flow into the fattening barn or slaughterhouse.

The Universal 5-Step Biological Flow

Every species in automatic mode follows the exact same chain:

[Adult Breeding Stock] 
         │
         ▼
  (Births / Eggs Laid)
         │
         ├───> [Replacements Retained] (to sustain adult breeding stock)
         │
         └───> [Surplus Animals] ──> Fattening / Slaughter Pool ──> [Standing Barn Places (IPCC AAP)]
  1. Start with Mature Breeding Animals: You declare only the adult breeding parents in livestock_census.csv.
  2. Calculate Offspring Born or Eggs Laid: Driven by biological reproduction: parturition intervals, prolificacy, litter size, or daily egg output and fertility.
  3. Deduct Replacements: The young animals required to replace culled or aged breeding stock are retained on the farm (replacement_rate).
  4. Direct the Surplus to Meat Production: All offspring not retained for replacement move into the fattening barn / slaughter pool.
  5. Convert Annual Slaughter Animals into Standing Barn Places (IPCC Formula): Meat animals do not stay on the farm for 365 days; they only occupy a barn place for their feeding duration (productive_period_days). Using the IPCC Average Annual Population (AAP) formula, herdr translates the total annual finished animals into the average number of occupied barn places on any given day:
    Standing Places (AAP) = Annual Slaughter Animals * (Days on Feed / 365)

3. Conceptual Differences Across Species

The differences between species in herdr are not arbitrary tool formulas, but direct reflections of four fundamental zootechnical and management concepts:

Concept A: Single Births vs. Multiple Litters vs. Continuous Egg Laying

  • Cattle (Single-birth monotocous):
    Cows have a long 9-month gestation and conceive a single calf. Therefore, the biological rhythm is strictly annual (at most 1 calving per cow per year). The main driver of births is the success of breeding: the pregnancy rate (pregnancy_rate), which is split equally (50:50) into male and female calves.
  • Sheep and Goats (Multiple-birth seasonal polytocous):
    Small ruminants have a shorter 5-month gestation. Farm managers can leverage two biological levers:
    1. Prolificacy (pr_sheep_goat): Multiple births per parturition (singles, twins, triplets).
    2. Parturition frequency: In traditional seasonal systems, ewes lamb once per calendar year (365-day cycle). In intensified systems with accelerated breeding schedules, the lambing interval is shortened (e.g., 200 days, yielding 1.825 lambings per ewe per year).
  • Swine (Continuous litter-bearing):
    Sows have high fecundity and are non-seasonal. The key driver is the farrowing interval (gestation + lactation + weaning-to-service interval, averaging 148.9 days, or 2.45 litters per sow per year) combined with a large weaned litter size (piglets_suckling).
  • Poultry (Continuous egg laying):
    Birds do not experience mammalian pregnancies or parturitions; they lay eggs continuously throughout a batch laying curve. In broiler breeder flocks, fertile hatching eggs (daily egg output multiplied by fertility rate) hatch into day-old chicks that move directly into broiler houses.

Concept B: Replacement Logic — Who Gets Replaced and How?

  • Ruminants (Cattle, Sheep, Goats):
    Adult breeding males (bulls, rams, bucks) live on the farm alongside breeding females. Consequently, the farm retains both female and male replacement offspring to ensure the generational renewal of both sexes (replacement_rate).
  • Swine:
    Internal herd replacement focuses exclusively on the future breeding mothers (replacement gilts and sows). Breeding boars are not raised from the fattening herd; modern swine units source specialized boars from external genetic multipliers or rely on artificial insemination.
  • Poultry:
    Commercial poultry flocks do not replace individual birds as they age. Flocks are managed in complete batches (all-in / all-out): the entire flock enters at the same age, lays throughout the batch cycle, and is depopulated all at once for slaughter.
    By default, replacement pullet requirements are derived from batch turnover (365/productive_period_days365 / \text{productive\_period\_days}). However, herdr also supports defining custom replacement rates for laying_hens and breeder_meat_hens in reproduction_parameters.csv for flexible multi-cycle or molting scenarios.

Concept C: Rearing Duration (One Year vs. Two Years)

  • Cattle:
    A replacement heifer takes over two years to reach adult breeding weight and deliver her first calf. Because of this extended growth period, the demographic model establishes two consecutive age tiers:
    1. Replacement calves (< 1 year of age): dairy_calves_female_replacement, beef_calves_*_replacement.
    2. Replacement yearlings (1 to 2 years of age): dairy_yearlings_female_replacement, beef_yearlings_*_replacement (mapped 1:1 from replacement calves).
  • Sheep, Goats, Swine, and Poultry:
    Young females reach reproductive maturity within their first year of life. They transition directly from growing replacements into productive adults without intermediate yearling tiers.

Concept D: The Dual Role of productive_period_days (Inter-Parturition Intervals vs. Life Cycles & AAP)

The parameter productive_period_days in livestock_weights.csv serves two distinct biological purposes depending on the animal cohort:

  1. For Adult Breeding Females (except laying hens): Inter-Parturition Interval
    For cows, ewes, does, and sows, productive_period_days represents the period between consecutive births (calving, lambing, kidding, or farrowing interval):

    • Cattle: Typically 365 days (or 365–400 days) for a single annual calving.
    • Sheep and Goats: 365 days in annual seasonal systems, or shortened (e.g., 200 to 240 days) in accelerated intensive breeding schedules.
    • Swine: Averages 149 days (115 d gestation + 21–28 d lactation + return to estrus), yielding 365/149≈2.45365 / 149 \approx 2.45 farrowings per sow per year.
      The annual reproduction frequency is calculated as 365/productive_period_days365 / \text{productive\_period\_days}.

  2. For Laying Hens & Poultry Breeders: Flock Laying Cycle
    Birds follow an all-in / all-out batch dynamic. productive_period_days represents the commercial laying cycle duration in the barn until depopulation (e.g., 511 days for commercial layers, 301 days for meat breeders). In the absence of an explicit replacement rate, flock turnover is 365/productive_period_days365 / \text{productive\_period\_days}.

  3. For All Other Cohorts (Growing, Fattening, and Replacement Stock): Life Cycle / Days on Feed
    For meat animals and rearing stock, productive_period_days represents their entire life-stage duration (days on feed from birth/weaning to slaughter or replacement transition; e.g., 42 days for broilers, 110 days for fattening pigs, 70 days for feedlot lambs).

    • Meat animals do not stay in the barn for 365 days. The package applies the IPCC Average Annual Population (AAP) principle:
      Standing Places (AAP)=Annual Slaughter Animals×(productive_period_days365)\text{Standing Places (AAP)} = \text{Annual Slaughter Animals} \times \left(\frac{\text{productive\_period\_days}}{365}\right)
    • It also determines the Average Daily Gain (ADG) used for energy and nitrogen retention calculations:
      ADG=BWfinal−BWinitialproductive_period_days\text{ADG} = \frac{BW_{final} - BW_{initial}}{\text{productive\_period\_days}}

4. Summary of Associated Parameter Columns

Species Base Adult Tag in livestock_census.csv Productivity Column & Source File Replacement Column & Source File Cycle Duration Column (productive_period_days in livestock_weights.csv)
Cattle mature_dairy_cattle, mature_beef_cattle, mature_beef_bull pregnancy_rate (ruminant_definitions.csv) replacement_rate (reproduction_parameters.csv — both sexes) Calving interval (e.g. 365 d) for cows; feeding duration for feedlot calves
Sheep mature_sheep_female_*, mature_sheep_male_* pr_sheep_goat (ruminant_definitions.csv) replacement_rate (reproduction_parameters.csv — both sexes) Lambing interval (e.g. 200–365 d) for ewes; feeding duration for lambs
Goats mature_goat_female_*, mature_goat_male_* pr_sheep_goat (ruminant_definitions.csv) replacement_rate (reproduction_parameters.csv — both sexes) Kidding interval (e.g. 200–365 d) for does; feeding duration for kids
Swine breeder_sows, boars piglets_suckling (monogastric_definitions.csv) replacement_rate (reproduction_parameters.csv — sows only) Farrowing interval (e.g. 149 d) for sows; feeding duration (110 d) for pigs
Poultry laying_hens, breeder_meat_hens fertility_rate, eggs_per_year (monogastric_definitions.csv) replacement_rate (reproduction_parameters.csv) Laying flock cycle (e.g. 511 d) for hens; life cycle (e.g. 42 d) for broilers
